items.title: Explainable AI for Streaming Process Mining: Overview, Challenges and Outlook
items.abstract: Streaming Process Mining (SPM) enables the real-time analysis of business processes through the continuous processing of event streams, providing timely insights and facilitating quick decisions. Although SPM supports various applications in multiple domain areas, it often relies on data-driven algorithms that lack interpretability, limiting user acceptance and trust. To tackle such shortcomings, explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) offers promising techniques to improve transparency and understanding of the applied approach. Despite their complementarity, SPM and XAI originate from distinct research communities, each with its own focus, methodologies, and evaluation criteria. This paper provides an overview of the intersection between XAI and SPM. We categorize existing work according to the SPM tasks addressed, the XAI methodologies used, and the level of interpretability from the end-user’s perspective. In addition, we identify key research challenges and propose future directions aimed at developing more human-centered and trustworthy SPM approaches. Our findings emphasize the importance of aligning algorithmic performance and human comprehension to support responsible decision making in dynamic process environments.

items.title: Exploring EFL students’ critical AI literacy in generative AI-assisted essay revision: insights into profiles and trajectories
items.abstract: This study examines how English as a foreign language (EFL) students demonstrate and develop Critical AI Literacy (CAIL) in generative AI-assisted essay revision. Drawing on the APSE model, which conceptualizes CAIL across four dimensions (awareness, positionality, interaction strategies, and evaluation), we conducted a longitudinal case study of three focal students across four writing tasks throughout a semester. Data sources included student-AI interaction logs, think-aloud protocols, stimulated recall interviews, and both initial and revised essay drafts. Qualitative analyses were conducted to trace patterns and changes in students’ CAIL. Findings show that all three students demonstrated CAIL across the four dimensions, although critical evaluation and critical positionality emerged as the most salient dimensions. Students selectively integrated AI feedback based on rhetorical fit, linguistic appropriateness, and factual accuracy, demonstrating various levels of agency. Over time, two students became increasingly selective and context-sensitive in their engagement with AI, whereas the third demonstrated strategic engagement from the outset but showed substantial task-to-task variation in feedback uptake. Overall, the students’ trajectories were heterogeneous and task-dependent rather than uniformly progressive. These patterns challenge linear models of AI literacy and highlight its situated nature in EFL writing contexts. Pedagogically, the study calls for differentiated instruction that fosters evaluative judgment and self-representation alongside prompt design. The findings contribute to a growing body of research advocating for more nuanced, learner-centered approaches to AI integration in foreign language writing.

items.title: Eye and Face Protection Violations Have Ranked Among OSHA’s Top 10 Since 2018: An Evidence-Based Framework for Intelligent Detection, Risk Assessment, and Timely Intervention
items.abstract: Eye and face protection violations under the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) standard have repeatedly appeared among the most frequently cited federal workplace safety standards since fiscal year 2018, highlighting persistent challenges in personal protective equipment (PPE) compliance, hazard recognition, and occupational safety management. Workers in construction, manufacturing, and other high-risk industrial environments remain vulnerable to eye and facial injuries arising from flying particles, chemical splashes, molten materials, dust, and other hazardous exposures. Although conventional workplace inspections, safety training, and supervisory monitoring remain essential, these approaches are often constrained by limited observation coverage, intermittent assessments, delayed identification of violations, and inconsistent enforcement. Advances in artificial intelligence (AI), computer vision, and edge computing offer opportunities to strengthen PPE monitoring through automated recognition, contextual risk assessment, and timely corrective intervention. This study examines the regulatory, technological, and operational challenges associated with persistent eye and face protection violations and develops an evidence-based framework for integrating AI-assisted PPE detection with proactive occupational safety management. Specifically, it investigates how deep learning-based object detection, worker–PPE association, pose estimation, edge inference, hazard-aware decision rules, and human-centered intervention mechanisms can improve the identification, prioritization, and resolution of potentially unsafe PPE practices. An evidence-based narrative synthesis was conducted using OSHA regulatory information and peer-reviewed literature addressing occupational eye and face injuries, PPE compliance monitoring, computer vision architectures, machine learning, workplace hazard assessment, and safety management systems. Particular attention was given to You Only Look Once (YOLO)-based detection models, pose and key point estimation, lightweight edge-computing architectures, temporal tracking, and multiclass PPE classification. Existing studies were critically examined to identify methodological strengths, operational limitations, performance variability, and research gaps. Building on the reviewed evidence, this study develops a risk-informed occupational eye and face protection assessment methodology that integrates regulatory requirements, hazard exposure, protective equipment adequacy, monitoring reliability, and corrective intervention effectiveness. Rather than proposing another automated PPE detection architecture, the methodology examines how technology-generated observations can be interpreted within task-specific safety requirements and translated into measurable intervention priorities. It distinguishes confirmed equipment absence, incorrect positioning, unsuitable protection, and insufficient visual evidence while incorporating mathematical indicators for hazard-weighted prioritization, detection reliability, corrective-action timeliness, and occupational injury incidence. Computer vision and edge-based monitoring are examined as supporting sources of safety evidence rather than independent injury-prevention solutions. The resulting methodology provides a structured basis for prospective evaluation of monitoring-supported safety interventions. No newly trained detection model, experimental dataset, or completed field trial is reported. Unlike conventional PPE recognition systems that primarily identify equipment presence, the framework emphasizes whether appropriate protective equipment is correctly positioned, associated with the exposed worker, and suitable for the prevailing occupational hazard. It also incorporates human oversight, privacy safeguards, explainable decision support, and mechanisms for managing false-positive detections and ambiguous visual conditions. The study proposes a multidimensional evaluation strategy extending beyond conventional computer vision metrics such as precision, recall, mean average precision, and inference speed. Recommended performance indicators include event-level violation detection sensitivity, false alerts per worker-hour, end-to-end notification latency, time to verified corrective action, unresolved hazardous exposure duration, recurrence of PPE violations, and longitudinal occupational injury outcomes. The proposed framework provides a structured basis for comparing AI-assisted monitoring with conventional safety inspection approaches while distinguishing technical detection performance from operational intervention effectiveness. It further identifies research priorities involving small-object recognition, transparent protective eyewear detection, cross-site generalizability, risk-based alert optimization, worker privacy, and prospective validation of injury-prevention outcomes. AI-assisted eye and face protection monitoring represents a promising approach to addressing persistent PPE compliance challenges through continuous observation, contextual violation assessment, and timely intervention. However, high detection accuracy and rapid alert generation alone do not demonstrate reductions in occupational injuries. Effective prevention requires reliable worker - PPE association, hazard-specific compliance assessment, accountable human intervention, verified corrective action, and integration with established occupational safety procedures. The proposed framework advances the conceptual foundation for transforming automated PPE recognition into a measurable, human-centered workplace safety intervention. Future empirical research should validate the framework across diverse industrial environments and determine whether improved violation detection and corrective-action timeliness translate into sustained reductions in hazardous exposure and preventable eye and face injuries.

items.title: FLUID: Flexible, Evidence-Grounded Situated Task Guidance
items.abstract: Real-time task guidance is inherently flexible: when an agent guides a user through a task, multiple responses and timings can be appropriate, and sometimes the best action is to remain silent. Existing benchmarks often miss this flexibility by treating synthesized dialogues as fixed targets for what to say and when to say it. We introduce FLUID (Flexible, Evidence-Grounded Situated Task Guidance), a unified framework for modeling, evaluating, and enabling flexible interaction in multimodal task guidance. Using naturally occurring human-human guidance from WTaG and HoloAssist, FLUID grounds interventions in their supporting evidence, necessity, and timing flexibility, and uses this representation both to evaluate flexible guidance and to build a real-time agent for task guidance. Our agent achieves the strongest overall balance of response correctness, intervention precision, timely guidance, and response latency among evaluated systems, while still leaving room for improvement in avoiding speech overlap. Together, FLUID moves situated task guidance beyond rigid reference matching toward more natural and adaptive human-AI interaction. Project page: https://fluid-guidance.github.io.

items.title: From AI Dialogue to Open Access: Making a Scholar's Foundational Works Accessible
items.abstract: This reflective case study documents how sustained collaboration with ChatGPT helped Jean-Pol Martin make his doctoral dissertation (1985) and habilitation thesis (1994) openly accessible. According to Martin’s retrospective account, AI dialogue introduced publication possibilities he had not previously considered and supported the organization of a process involving digitization, publisher permission, legal assistance and coordination with the University Library of Eichstätt-Ingolstadt. Over approximately two months, at a reported cost of EUR 400, both foundational works were made available through Zenodo and the university’s publication server, KU.edoc. The dissertation’s two microfiche supplements were also digitized and published. Inclusion of the digital editions in the library catalogue was pending at the reporting cut-off. The paper examines the complementary contributions of AI assistance, human initiative and institutional infrastructure. Its contribution to the ongoing exploration of Martin’s human-AI model is a documented implementation process whose outputs extend beyond jointly generated text: publicly accessible primary sources. The study distinguishes demonstrated accessibility from potential future effects on discovery, scholarly reception and citation impact. It also addresses limitations concerning retrospective testimony, machine readability and long-term preservation. Prepared with ChatGPT assistance; presented as a reflective working paper, not as peer-reviewed research.

items.title: From Fields Medalists' Concerns to Hidden Capture: A Tale of Two Simulated Worlds of Human Cognition
items.abstract: Hidden capture is a loss of skill that the people losing it do not notice, combined with a dependence that does not reverse when the pressure behind it eases. The Correction Freeze Problem predicts this pattern, but testing it on human thinking would take decades of data that do not yet exist for generative AI. We therefore built a computer simulation of a population, calibrated to what can be measured today, and followed it across generations in two worlds that share the same machines. In World M, AI mostly replaces people’s own practice, and each generation learns what normal ability looks like from the one before. In World N, AI mostly supports practice, and each generation’s sense of normal ability is anchored in direct experience, including time in nature. The model reproduces today’s rise of AI-written text in student work, the share of people who check AI output, and how loosely people’s opinions of their own thinking track tested performance. The simulations show what a captured world would be like from the inside. Delegation stays modest for a while and then sweeps through most of the population within a few years, because each person who hands over their thinking makes it more normal for everyone else. Skill then drains away without being felt. In World M, the average person’s unaided ability fell to about the bottom tenth of the population before AI, yet people registered only a small part of that loss, about a quarter even a century later, because their machine-assisted work looked as good as ever and everyone around them had declined too. The habit of checking disappeared first: at full delegation, only two people in a hundred still compared the machine’s answers with their own judgment, and when the machine’s error rate was quietly doubled, about one in a hundred noticed within five years. In an illustrative century, easing the pressure after a generation of heavy delegation restored only World N; the other two worlds were still captured half a century later. Staying out of the trap proved far easier than climbing out of it. These findings are conditional projections, not forecasts. Across 2,176 sensitivity runs, the unseen loss appeared every time, and its size depended mainly on two things societies can influence now: whether AI replaces or supports people’s own practice, and whether each generation anchors its sense of competence in direct experience. Whether capture can be undone depended on one quantity not yet measured, how much an individual’s reliance on AI changes from year to year; if reliance churns, capture becomes reversible, though it stays hidden. Several earlier results weakened as the model was corrected, and the main pre-specified test of a final extension came back negative; both are reported.

items.title: From psychological needs to knowledge practices: individual inquiry and shared learning in generative AI-supported vocational education
items.abstract: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) provides rapid access to explanations and examples, but information access does not necessarily become effective learning. Drawing on self-determination theory, this study examined associations among autonomy, competence, and relatedness need satisfaction, knowledge acquisition, knowledge sharing, and perceived learning effectiveness. Methods A cross-sectional survey included 300 adult students in computing-related programs at seven vocational colleges in Nanchang, China. The common reference was learning in web design and development during the preceding 4 weeks. Confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling were complemented by fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA). Results All three psychological needs were positively associated with knowledge acquisition. Autonomy and competence were significantly associated with knowledge sharing; the relatedness coefficient was positive but did not reach the 0.05 significance level. Acquisition and sharing were both positively associated with perceived learning effectiveness. Autonomy and competence had significant statistical indirect associations through both practices, whereas relatedness had a significant indirect association only through acquisition. These separate significance tests do not establish differences between coefficients. Three configurations were associated with high perceived effectiveness, two of which included relatedness. Low-outcome configurations remained exploratory because their proportional reduction in inconsistency values fell below the specified threshold. Discussion GenAI was the contextual framing rather than an independently measured exposure, and the knowledge practices were not exclusive to GenAI. The outcome was subjective, and neither the indirect paths nor the configurations establish causality or objective learning gains.

items.title: From Shoebox to Toolbox: Archival Affirmation in the AI-Assisted Processing of a Media-Art Archive
items.abstract: Large digitised media collections often remain unprocessed and unexplored, despite being technically preserved, and archival institutions increasingly turn to artificial intelligence (AI). Rather than pursuing autonomous archival systems, this article examines how AI can support archival description and classification while preserving the contextual, historical and provenance-related integrity of archival materials. Drawing on the archive of media artist Teoman Madra (1931–2025), the study develops and evaluates an AI-assisted archival tool for a large, initially unstructured collection. The proposed approach establishes an iterative, human-in-the-loop workflow in which AI-generated suggestions are critically assessed by the archivist, whose decisions subsequently inform the system's outputs. The study shows that the controlled vocabulary given to the model shapes what it can recognise, that the archivist's validated decisions guide classification reliably within an archival unit but not across units, and that the model's contribution declines as tasks demand contextual knowledge beyond what is visible. While this process can improve efficiency and reveal details a person might miss, it also introduces epistemic risks, particularly when plausible but inaccurate classifications remain undetected. Faster processing does not by itself mean more reliable description. The article conceptualises AI-assisted archival classification as archival affirmation, a collaborative process in which human judgement remains integral to the production and validation of archival knowledge. By situating the archivist's interpretive authority at the centre of this process, the article contributes to discussions of the responsible integration, critical oversight and governance of AI in archival practice.

items.title: FROM THE AGE OF REASON TO THE AGE OF ALGORITHM
items.abstract: Eliyas Kebede Zemedkun, in his treatise From the Age of Reason to the Age of Algorithm, critically examines human sociocultural and political evolution, tracing the shift from mythological bewilderment and the worship of Logos to empiricism and the ultimate apotheosis of the algorithm. The author shows how truth migrated from God and mind to machines, leaving humanity excluded from knowledge production to become mere receivers. This technological deity operates as both servant and master, subsuming divine and demonic traits under automated architectures.Addressing the post human predicament, Zemedkun argues that surrendering truth, justice, and religion to algorithms evacuates human agency. Surveillance capitalism shifts from physical labor exploitation to cognitive exploitation, harvesting human thoughts, language, and art to train artificial intelligence models. Through the automation paradox, artificial intelligence accelerates capitalist self destruction by displacing industrial labor and eviscerating public purchasing capacity. Applying Nietzschean philosophy and the master slave dialectic, the author warns that delegating thought kills the will to power, creating the Last Man and reducing future generations to prompting animals. Foucault disciplinary power, Marcuse one dimensional digital man, and Derrida textual deconstruction trap humanity in simulated reason, shifting the paradigm from I think therefore I am to I prompt therefore I am.To rescue the general will from digital anarchy, Zemedkun introduces the Information Contract as a reciprocal normative commitment among citizens and institutions to protect information integrity based on mutual veracity. Distinguishing state formation as hardware from nation building as software, the author emphasizes that sustainable nations require information integrity rather than foundations built on myths. Concluding that the cognitive will to truth is what has died, Zemedkun asserts that society must embrace the Information Contract to avoid collapsing into a digital Hobbesian state of nature.

items.title: GenAI as an International Critical Peer: Expanding Perspectives in Learning
items.abstract: Generative AI is commonly used to generate answers, assist writing, and provide feedback. This article develops another educational role: the international critical peer for educators. In this role, educators use GenAI to surface assumptions and identify alternative interpretations when planning, designing, or making decisions across cultural and educational contexts. Drawing on work in global competence, intercultural competence, global citizenship education, and GenAI-supported critical feedback, this article presents a guided inquiry process for educators. The process begins with a real question, uses GenAI to surface possibilities, examines those possibilities through relevant evidence and input from people with experience in the setting, and then returns to the original decision. The aim is to expand professional inquiry while keeping interpretation and judgment with the educator.

items.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence in Doctoral Education: A Participatory Action Research Evaluation of the Dr. I.D.E.A. Model
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping doctoral education, yet few empirically evaluated pedagogical models integrate AI literacy with research and teaching competence. This study examined changes associated with implementing the Dr. I.D.E.A. Model, which positions doctoral candidates who are also university teachers as co-researchers of their own research and teaching practice under an explicit responsible-AI framework. A participatory action research design with convergent triangulation was implemented during the 2025–2026 academic year. Thirty-four doctoral candidates participated in four collaborative virtual workshops organised through cycles of planning, action, observation and critical reflection. Self-report measures administered at three time points were integrated with interviews, focus groups, observation notes, reflective logbooks and independently verified academic products. Self-reported research competence, AI-supported digital competence and creative-pedagogical competence increased significantly between each pair of measurement points (pre–post dₐᵥ = 1.83, 2.10 and 1.69, respectively). All participants integrated generative AI into at least one university course, and 76.5% implemented a sustained course redesign. Because the design lacked a comparison group and relied on perceived competence, maturation, testing effects, response-shift bias and the programme’s ordinary activities may also account for the changes. The findings are therefore associative rather than causal and constitute preliminary evidence that warrants controlled replication in other doctoral contexts.

items.title: Goal-Guided Reinforcement Learning via Fine-Tuning Vision-Language Models
items.abstract: Exploration remains a major challenge for reinforcement learning (RL) agents in Craftax-style environments due to sparse rewards and long horizons. Large language models (LLMs) can guide exploration by generating high-level goals, but methods using models without explicit task adaptation often rely on carefully designed prompts and may produce inconsistent or contextually inappropriate goals. We introduce CCGP-2M, a multimodal goal-preference dataset constructed from interaction trajectories in Craftax-Classic, and propose a vision-language model (VLM)-guided RL framework that learns environment-specific goal guidance from this dataset. The framework consists of two stages: offline VLM fine-tuning and online goal-guided RL. In the offline stage, we align the VLM with goal preferences using Kullback-Leibler Token-level Direct Preference Optimization (KLTDPO), which combines token-level KL regularization with distributionally robust reweighting. Experiments on Craftax-Classic show that our method collects diamonds earlier than state-of-the-art baselines, achieves the highest score and reward, and attains the highest success rates on most achievements.

items.title: Ground Truth Bias in AI-Assisted Medical Annotation: A Crossover Study Using an Independent Radiologist Reference Standard
items.abstract: Behavioural evaluations of artificial-intelligence-assisted annotation score every human decision against a reference standard, so their conclusions inherit that standard's validity. We tested how far conclusions about assistance, reliance and individual differences depend on it. Fifty-one non-expert high-school students annotated 50 knee radiographs for osteoarthritis, with and without a deliberately imperfect classifier, in a crossover design; personality and non-verbal reasoning were also measured. Decisions were scored against the public repository labels and against an independent reference standard from a radiologist panel, which graded 23 of the 50 images as indeterminate. Against the repository labels, assistance raised accuracy from 60.4% to 65.3% (odds ratio 1.23, p=0.002). Against the independent standard, the gain on the 27 determinate images was smaller and not significant in the primary model (78.4% to 80.8%; odds ratio 1.16, p=0.178). The apparent benefit had been concentrated on the indeterminate images and was not significant when those images were assigned to either class. The direction of residual over-reliance depended on how indeterminate cases were handled, and the personality trait most strongly associated with accuracy changed identity and sign between standards. Reliance measures are only as valid as the reference standard that defines when the assistant is right.

items.title: How to hire Claude Code developers
items.abstract: Choosing an AI model for business is not simply about picking the most popular platform or the model with the strongest benchmark score. Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini can all support business teams, but they differ in how they handle reasoning, writing, multimodal tasks, integrations, and ecosystem compatibility. The best AI model for business is the one that fits your actual workflows, data requirements, and long-term AI strategy. What makes an AI model suitable for business? Different teams expect different things from AI. Some companies may need strong writing and analysis capabilities, while others may prioritize multimodal workflows, automation, internal knowledge support, or integration with existing tools. That is why an AI model comparison for business should focus on practical use cases rather than model popularity alone. Teams need to understand how each option performs in the environments where it will actually be used. Comparing Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini are all capable AI platforms, but they are not interchangeable. Their strengths may differ depending on the type of work being performed and the ecosystem in which the company operates. For example, one model may be a better fit for long-form reasoning or content generation, while another may be stronger for multimodal tasks, integrations, or workflows connected to a particular technology stack. A useful comparison should therefore look at capabilities in the context of real business tasks. Choosing the right AI model Choosing the right AI model starts with understanding the problem you want AI to solve. Instead of adopting a platform because competitors are using it, businesses should identify the workflows where AI can provide measurable value. This may include internal knowledge support, content creation, research, data analysis, automation, or customer-facing tools. Once the use case is clear, teams can compare model capabilities, costs, integration options, and operational requirements more effectively. Enterprise considerations For larger organizations, the decision becomes more complex. An enterprise AI model comparison should consider not only performance, but also security, compliance, governance, scalability, integration requirements, and user adoption. The model may eventually become part of daily operations across several departments, which means long-term maintainability and compatibility with internal systems matter just as much as individual features. Final thoughts There is no single best AI model for business that works for every company. Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini each offer different strengths, and the right choice depends on how AI will be used inside the organization. By focusing on real workflows, integration requirements, security expectations, scalability, and business goals, companies can make a more practical AI model comparison for business and choose a platform that supports both current needs and future AI adoption.

items.title: Human authorship in artificial intelligence-assisted research: A counterfactual boundary test
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) can already participate in literature retrieval, question generation, coding, analysis, interpretation, and manuscript production, making fixed task-based rules about what should remain human increasingly unstable. This conceptual article introduces a Counterfactual Boundary Test for distinguishing why human involvement is retained in AI-assisted research. The test asks whether the rationale for human involvement would disappear if the relevant AI limitation disappeared. If so, the ground is capability-contingent; if the rationale persists because the work continues to be substantively attributed to human authors, the ground is human-authorship-related; other ethical, legal, fiduciary, political, or social grounds may remain distinct. Current hallucination and verification risks illustrate the first case, whereas comprehension, critical evaluation, justified acceptance, and accountability provide a parsimonious diagnostic synthesis for examining the second. The framework does not claim that all future science must remain human. Instead, it clarifies which rationales may move with technological capability and which arise specifically under human-authored science. These indicators do not replace the cumulative International Committee of Medical Journal Editors (ICMJE) authorship criteria. A worked citation-validation example illustrates selective revision of controls, and a specialist-coauthor case explains justified reliance.

items.title: Human-centred AI pedagogy in primary mathematics: a theoretical framework for agency and sense-making
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) can expand the resources available for primary mathematics teaching, but assisted task completion is not the same as mathematical learning. This article develops a Human-Centred AI Pedagogy Framework through a synthesis of sociocultural theory and humans-with-media, human-centred AI and hybrid intelligence, social cognitive theory, TPACK and its AI extensions, and Ubuntu-informed relational ethics. The framework connects pedagogical intentionality, teacher agency, learner agency, mathematical sense-making, and ethical and relational responsibility. Its proposed explanatory contribution concerns the destination of mathematical decisions in a teacher–child–AI relationship. When teachers reduce direct guidance, decisions may be delegated to children or taken over by the system; this paper describes the latter possibility as decision drift. Agency handover, therefore, means increasing children's supported responsibility for strategy, representation, justification, and help-seeking, while teachers retain safeguarding and instructional accountability. The dimensions are differentiated as prerequisites, enabling conditions, mediating processes, outcomes and ethical boundaries. Two hypothetical lessons, on Grade 3 place value and Grade 5 growing patterns, illustrate the framework and compare AI-supported and non-AI alternatives. South African multilingualism, unequal infrastructure and teacher workload specify important implementation conditions. Five propositions identify expected relationships, observable indicators and competing explanations, providing a basis for classroom observation and comparative studies. Evidence from older learners motivates the analysis but does not establish effects in primary classrooms. The framework's explanatory and predictive validity remains to be tested; its value is a more precise account of what AI-mediated mathematical activity should enable, protect and make open to investigation.

items.title: Human-first learning: scaffolding reasoning before AI assistance improves diagnostic accuracy
items.abstract: Generative AI could improve physicians' clinical performance, yet its use in medical training raises questions about whether trainees can develop the clinical reasoning needed to use AI effectively and independently. We conducted a longitudinal randomised controlled trial involving 496 medical students (389 analysed). Students completed clinical reasoning tasks with virtual standardised patients and were randomised to six conditions: no intervention, an AI assistant alone, AI scaffolding alone, scaffolding followed by the AI assistant, the AI assistant followed by scaffolding, or both simultaneously. AI scaffolding prompted students to reflect on and evaluate their reasoning without providing direct answers; the assistant provided requested information and answers. The study comprised an AI-free baseline, two intervention phases and a final assessment after all AI support was withdrawn. Frontier large language models (LLMs) completed the same tasks as an additional benchmark. Students initially performed below LLMs but later exceeded them following the interventions. Students who began with AI scaffolding achieved higher diagnostic accuracy than those given access to the AI assistant from the outset both during the subsequent intervention phase (75.2% vs 66.0%; OR 1.73, 95% CIs [1.12–2.68]) and after withdrawal (24.6% vs 14.4%; OR 2.19, 95% CIs [1.15–4.14]). After withdrawal, scaffold-first groups were the only groups to outperform both unsupported students (24.5–24.7% vs 9.0%; ORs 3.77–3.87, 95% CIs [1.25–12.00]) and LLMs (24.5–24.7% vs 8.6%; ORs 3.48–3.50, 95% CIs [1.22–9.89]). Introducing the AI assistant after scaffolding decreased intrinsic cognitive load ( t (50) = 3.25, p BH = .006, Cohen’s d z = 0.46, 95% CIs [0.17, 0.75]) and increased metacognitive evaluation ( t (50) = 3.11, p BH = .019, Cohen’s d z = 0.44, 95% CIs [0.15, 0.73]). These findings support a staged and human-first approach to AI use in medical training, in which reasoning-focused scaffolding precedes answer-providing assistance to strengthen diagnostic performance both during AI-supported learning and after AI support is withdrawn.

items.title: Human–AI Cybersecurity Decision Loops: The Effect of AI Reliability on Human Vigilance
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly being integrated into cybersecurity systems to support threat detection, security monitoring, incident analysis, and decision-making. The ability of AI systems to process large volumes of security information and provide rapid recommendations can improve the efficiency of cybersecurity operations. However, the increasing dependence on AI may also influence how humans evaluate security information and respond to potential threats. In particular, differences in AI reliability may affect user trust, confidence, independent verification, and vigilance during cybersecurity decision-making. This paper examines the relationship between AI reliability and human vigilance in AI-assisted cybersecurity decision loops, with particular attention to trust, decision accuracy, confidence, verification behaviour, and human judgement. Drawing on existing literature related to human-AI collaboration, automation bias, cybersecurity decision-making, trust in AI, and cognitive behaviour, the paper develops a conceptual framework linking AI reliability, human trust, cognitive vigilance, verification behaviour, and cybersecurity decision quality. The paper considers AI as a decision-support mechanism rather than a complete replacement for human judgement. While reliable AI recommendations may support faster and more effective decisions, inappropriate reliance on AI may reduce independent evaluation and increase the possibility of accepting incorrect recommendations. The proposed framework provides a basis for future empirical research examining how different levels of AI reliability influence human vigilance and decision-making in cybersecurity environments.

items.title: Independent Learning after Generative AI Support in School Mathematics: A Systematic Review and Assessment-Stratified Meta-Analysis
items.abstract: Background and Objective. Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) solves school math problems on demand. Higher scores during live tool access do not prove retained mathematical competence once that support disappears. Earlier meta-analyses pooled assisted task completion together with unmonitored and closed-book posttests, which obscured whether pupils actually learned to work alone. This PRISMA 2020 systematic review and stratified meta-analysis evaluates K–12 mathematics outcomes by separating test-time resource rules from instructional design. Methods. Two-stream searches across ERIC, APA PsycNet, OpenAlex, Crossref, Semantic Scholar, arXiv, EuropePMC, and bidirectional citation chasing (1 January 2022–8 November 2026) returned 11,061 raw entries and 6,530 unique records. Every sought report was retrieved in full (372 / 372; 0 unretrieved). Eligibility verification and mathematical consistency checks retained 49 K–12 school-mathematics reports across 46 independent cohorts and supplied 36 quantitative contrasts across 20 controlled study families (21 controlled quantitative reports, plus 1 factorial within-AI modality trial synthesized narratively) alongside 28 qualitative, single-arm, observational, and boundary-comparator reports. Random-effects Paule–Mandel and restricted maximum likelihood estimators with classroom cluster adjustments (calibrated intraclass correlation ρ = 0.128) stratified contrasts across Category A (GenAI active during testing), Category B (posttest with undocumented resource rules), Category C (partial human-help restriction), and Category D (explicit closedresource immediate and delayed exams). Results. Within primary multi-cluster and individually randomized trials (k = 14), large concurrent gains during live GenAI access (Category A: g = +0.615, 95% CI [+0.044, +1.185], p = .035) shrank across undocumented posttests (Category B: g = +0.186 [+0.009, +0.362]) and tutor-restricted exit tickets (Category C: g = +0.095 [+0.024, +0.167]) down to a tight null on explicit closed-resource exams (Category D: g = −0.010 [−0.137, +0.117], p = .876; focal contrast Δg = +0.625, p = .036). Extended controlled trials (k = 28) confirmed strong between-category moderation (Q_between = 12.55, p = .0059; Category D: g = −0.035 [−0.149, +0.078]). Pedagogical architecture accounted for all primary post-withdrawal heterogeneity (Q_between = 18.69, p = .0001; I² = 0% within every tier). Unconstrained direct-answer access harmed closed-exam scores (M1: g = −0.205, p = .043), passive hint guardrails blocked harm without yielding net transfer (M2: g = −0.038, p = .173), and architectures enforcing productive cognitive friction (unaided mastery gating, teachable agents, Socratic Pólya scaffolding, and human-in-the-loop oversight) produced durable gains (M3: g = +0.100, p = .0001; extended g = +0.315, p = .0002). Head-to-head within-AI trials (k = 6) favored pedagogical guardrails and teacher mediation over unguarded GenAI (g = +0.645 [+0.215, +1.075], p = .0033), whereas upper-secondary algebra and calculus cohorts showed acute offloading and workingmemory overload. Conclusions. Unstratified, unclustered synthesis inflates verified closed-resource mathematics learning by +0.26 to +0.29 SD (naive g = +0.275 vs. closed-resource g = −0.010). Durable competence requires crossing two distinct thresholds. Instructional systems must block direct answer copying and enforce active learner generation before and after AI withdrawal.

items.title: Influence of User Experience on Perceptions of the Reliability of Lesson Plans Generated by Generative AI
items.abstract: The emergence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is transforming pedagogical practices in Cameroonian secondary education. This study assesses the influence of teachers' experience using GenAI tools on how secondary school teachers in Yaoundé perceive the reliability and compliance of generated content with the guidelines of the Competency-Based Approach (CBA). Using a sequential explanatory mixed-methods design, 370 teachers were surveyed by questionnaire and 130 others through semi-structured interviews (total N = 500). The Chi-square test reveals a highly significant association between GenAI user status and the perception of the quality of generated content (χ 2 (3) = 41.527; p < 0.001; Cramer's V = 0.335). Among users, 33.46% described the content as "contextual" compared to 15.38% of non-users. The interviews explain this difference through the progressive learning of contextual prompt engineering. However, 65.9% of all respondents judged the generated lesson plans to be poorly compliant with CBA guidelines. The study concludes that while direct experience improves the perception of GenAI, the structural deficit in African contextualization of large language models remains a major obstacle, which only targeted prompt engineering training and the development of better-adapted tools will be able to overcome.

items.title: Information Overload and Disutility in Generative AI Systems as Cognitive Extension: A Bounded Rationality Perspective
items.abstract: Generative AI systems promise cognitive extensions by enhancing information access and use. However, from the bounded rationality perspective, their utility is fundamentally constrained by inherent human cognitive limitations. This article argues that when the volume of AI-generated information exceeds users’ processing capacity governed by working memory constraints, attentional resources, and verification capabilities, it produces cognitive disutility rather than enhancement. We introduced a formal model to quantify this interaction, demonstrating that net cognitive benefits decline systematically as information overload increases beyond individual processing thresholds. The analysis reveals that successful cognitive extension depends not on maximizing informational output but on strategically aligning AI design with human cognitive ergonomics and individual differences in processing capacity. Ultimately, truly augmentative systems must minimize cognitive overhead to prevent overload, while preserving users' epistemic agency and decision-making autonomy.

items.title: Insights on the implementation barriers of the learning methods deployment in oncology: a review
items.abstract: This review systematically identifies and synthesizes implementation barriers reported in the literature regarding artificial intelligence (AI)-based decision support systems in oncology. Following PRISMA guidelines, an initial search of the Scopus and PubMed databases and a subsequent citation-prioritized update identified review articles published between January 2021 and December 2025, of which 113 met the inclusion criteria. The review addresses five interconnected barriers: model interpretability, external validation, fairness and class imbalance, electronic health record integration, and data standardization. External validation is the most frequently cited challenge (73.5%), followed by model interpretability (66.4%) and data standardization (65.5%). Temporal trends show a marked increase in validation concerns, from 56.7% in 2021 to 93.8% in 2025, and declining attention to fairness barriers, from 53.3% in 2021 to 37.5% in 2025. This paper makes four main contributions. First, it presents an integrative framework showing that the barriers form an interconnected system in which fairness propagates into all downstream components, so that the observed decline in explicit fairness research signals a critical gap in current priorities. Second, it quantifies barrier prevalence and its temporal evolution, enabling evidence-based prioritization. Third, it consolidates the approaches reported in the literature into unified pipelines for bias mitigation and model interpretation. Fourth, it proposes a stage-specific implementation protocol with a decision flowchart to guide barrier assessment before deployment in screening, diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis applications. The findings indicate that effective AI implementation in oncology requires addressing multiple barriers simultaneously rather than in isolation. The proposed frameworks and implementation protocol provide actionable guidance for researchers and practitioners working to translate AI models from development to clinical practice.

items.title: Intelligent Learning Systems: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Transforming Education
items.abstract: AI is slowly changing how education is planned, delivered and assessed. With machine learning, natural language processing and learning analytics, a platform can respond better to the different needs of its students. This paper looks at what AI can do in education and sets out a conceptual framework for an intelligent learning environment, one that combines learner information, adaptive materials, automated feedback and guidance from teachers. It covers personalised learning, intelligent tutoring, regular assessment, early identification of learning difficulties and accessibility. It also takes up the concerns that come with these tools: student privacy, bias, unequal access to technology, inaccurate AI-generated content, academic honesty and overdependence. The paper rests on a focused review of selected academic and policy literature. It reports no new experiment and no original student data. Its argument is that AI can make learning more supportive and flexible when used responsibly, and that it should assist teachers and students rather than replace the judgement, effort and human contact that education depends on.

items.title: Is AI Governing Us? A Deep Dive into the Regulatory Gaps in Bangladeshi AI Governance
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is widespread throughout the world and is used, knowingly and unknowingly, because of the speed of its services. People live under an illusion about AI’s advancement, which creates profound barriers to human security in the digital world, harms people in the real world and creates risks to fundamental human rights. In response to this risk, the European Union has adopted a significant regulatory model, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (the EU AI Act). The Act prohibits several AI practices, such as manipulation, and provides risk-based protection so that AI systems are transparent and accountable to people and governments. As a result, AI systems can be reconciled with human safety, security and the protection of fundamental rights. However, incidents of AI manipulation have occurred, including the violation of a child’s right to life, and many other incidents are taking place, especially affecting vulnerable AI users, because many countries lack binding legal protection. Legislation on AI is not limited to technological innovation but also concerns human security, transparency and accountability. Bangladesh produced the draft National Artificial Intelligence Policy 2024 (NAIP) and later the National AI Policy 2026–2030 (Draft v2.0), which provides some important protections for human lives against AI manipulation, including data protection and cybersecurity, grounded in Bangladeshi culture. However, the policy focuses on public services, innovation and economic growth, primarily to fulfil the technological ambitions of Vision 2041 in line with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Consequently, human security and protection from AI remain an option rather than a primary goal among the policy’s commitments. Not only Bangladesh but most South Asian countries lack protection for people, especially the vulnerable, against AI manipulation. This qualitative legal research therefore examines the adequacy of AI governance and enforcement in Bangladesh in protecting digital security and fundamental rights. Drawing comparative insights from the EU AI Act, it examines gaps in Bangladesh’s digital legislation and institutional practice and identifies best practices. It also compares practice in the neighbouring countries of India and Pakistan to assess Bangladesh’s position within South Asia’s regional AI governance framework. Through a critical analysis of primary and secondary sources, it finds that Bangladesh and its neighbours have adopted policies but lack adequate protections and binding laws to govern AI systems, leaving people living blindfolded.

items.title: Knowledge, attitudes and practices regarding artificial intelligence among pharmacy students in Guinea and Malawi: a cross-national, multicentre cross-sectional study
items.abstract: Background Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has entered pharmacy education faster than curricula have adapted, yet evidence on how pharmacy students in sub-Saharan Africa understand and use it is almost absent. We assessed knowledge, attitudes and practices (KAP) regarding AI among pharmacy students in a Francophone (Guinea) and an Anglophone (Malawi) country, and identified their determinants. Methods A multicentre online cross-sectional survey (29 March–12 June 2026) included pharmacy students from three universities in Conakry, Guinea, and from Kamuzu University of Health Sciences, Malawi. A bilingual self-administered questionnaire measured knowledge (9 items), attitudes (8 Likert items) and practices (7 items, score 0–11). Prespecified cut-offs defined adequate knowledge (≥ 70%), favourable attitude (≥ 75%) and adequate practice (≥ 8/11). Multivariable logistic regression models, structured along the KAP pathway, estimated adjusted odds ratios (aOR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Results Of 322 participants (Guinea 115, Malawi 207; median age 23 years), 99.7% had heard of AI and 96.2% had used AI tools, but only 27.9% had received formal AI training. Adequate knowledge was found in 32.0% (95% CI 27.1–37.3), favourable attitudes in 30.2% (25.4–35.4) and adequate practices in 64.3% (58.9–69.3). Half of the students (49.8%) believed that AI always provides correct results, and only 18.9% always verified AI-generated information. The two countries showed mirror-image profiles: Malawian students knew AI applications better and were more favourable to AI (aOR 3.77; 1.79–7.97), whereas Guinean students more often recognised AI's limitations and verified its outputs. Adequate practice was independently associated with adequate knowledge (aOR 2.28; 1.26–4.13) and favourable attitude (aOR 2.57; 1.40–4.73), and inversely with age > 23 years (aOR 0.39; 0.21–0.74) and studying in Malawi (aOR 0.39; 0.19–0.81). Advanced years of study predicted adequate knowledge (≥ 5th year: aOR 4.62; 1.27–16.87), while self-reported formal AI training was not associated with better knowledge. Conclusions Pharmacy students in both countries use AI almost universally but lack the critical knowledge needed to use it safely, with a high risk of automation bias. Curricula should move beyond tool familiarity towards structured, competency-based AI literacy centred on output verification, limitations, ethics and pharmacist accountability, adapted to each national context.

items.title: L2 Writers’ Generative AI Use Boosts Writing Quality, but not Uniformly: Cases of No Improvement
items.abstract: Although artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI (GenAI), has been widely discussed in second language writing research as a promising form of support, earlier studies have not compared the quality of the same writers’ work when they compose with and without it. Furthermore, it remains uncertain whether GenAI consistently enhances writing quality across individuals. The present study employs both quantitative and qualitative approaches to assess whether GenAI improves the analytic quality of individual second language writers’ essays and to explore whether, and if so, why certain writers’ experience declines in particular components of writing quality. All participants completed two essays in a fixed sequence, first without GenAI assistance and then with it, which may constitute a potential limitation of the study design. The quantitative analyses indicated that, overall, essays written with GenAI assistance received higher scores across all four analytic components (task response, coherence and cohesion, lexical resource, and grammatical range and accuracy) than essays written without GenAI assistance. Yet this pattern was not consistent; some writers actually declined on specific components. The qualitative analyses then identified three themes that explain lower scores in particular domains when GenAI was used: (1) the prioritization of content and evidence during GenAI interaction over the management of the overall demands of the task, which led to inadequate task fulfillment and formatting; (2) the inclusion of GenAI suggestions without sufficient attention to integration or coherence; and (3) a relative lack of attention to vocabulary and grammar revision. These results point to the importance of instructional interventions that support effective GenAI use and AI literacy among second language writers, and suggest that GenAI-based systems should be customized to align with writers’ specific needs and the specific components of task requirements.

items.title: Law at the Speed of AI: Critical Legal Infrastructure for the Machine Age: Autonomy Under Law Architecture (AULA)
items.abstract: The global deployment of autonomous AI agents within and across organisations exceeds the governance infrastructure available to constrain it. Agent communication and authentication protocols, principally the Model Context Protocol and the Agent2Agent Protocol, are maturing quickly, but maturity at the protocol layer does not produce legal legibility at the governance layer. Runtime enforcement written by the deploying organisation fixes the resources an AI agent can reach, not the authority under which it acts. Legal legibility is the capacity of a legal system to recognise, interpret and regulate activity by mapping it onto legal personhood, property, rights and liabilities. Existing (analogue) legal infrastructure cannot supply it for autonomous deployment. The resulting deficit is bidirectional. It concerns the attribution of liability when an AI agent causes harm, and the allocation of rights, including data and economic rights, generated by agentic activity and by the AI agent itself as a source of value and form of property. This paper characterises that deficit as the legal attribution gap, a material and unaddressed risk to economies, organisations and citizens that is magnified in cross-organisational multi-agent deployment. The paper describes the Autonomy Under Law Architecture (AULA), in which AI systems and data assets are registered as legal objects anchored to one or more identified legal persons, governed by cryptographically tethered smart legal instruments and evaluated at runtime. Each smart legal instrument can carry a legal context clause, through which the legislation, regulation and judicial decisions in force at the time of the act are given practical and legal effect in that evaluation. Infrastructure of this kind is a precondition for the continued function of any legal, property and economic system with both human and autonomous machine stakeholders.

items.title: Learner Autonomy and Critical Thinking in AI-Assisted Adult Learning
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly entering adult and continuing education, where it can explain, summarise, draft and evaluate on the learner's behalf. The quality of work produced with AI assistance may therefore rise while the learner's own understanding, judgement and critical thinking remain unchanged or decline. This conceptual article examines how AI-assisted adult learning can preserve learner autonomy, independent judgement and critical thinking while still benefiting from generative tools. It builds on Natseva's distinction between functional cognitive offloading and higher-order cognitive outsourcing and integrates it with research on learner autonomy, self-regulated learning, metacognition, automation bias, critical-thinking instruction and the learning–performance distinction, drawing on a purposive, non-systematic literature selection that is reported transparently. Because most empirical studies of generative AI in education involve school or university students, the article distinguishes evidence by learner population and discusses its transferability to adult education. The original contribution is the AI-Assisted Autonomy and Critical Thinking Assessment (AACTA) framework, which specifies six assessable dimensions: prior independent reasoning, purposeful AI engagement, appraisal of AI output, cross-source contrast, decision ownership, and unaided demonstration and transfer. Each dimension is operationalised as a scoring rubric with observable indicators at three levels, from displaced to autonomous, together with a procedure for training two assessors and checking their agreement. AACTA is compared with existing measures of learner autonomy, self-regulated learning and critical thinking. The framework is accompanied by a dual-outcome principle, which requires AI-assisted performance and unaided learning to be measured separately, and by a provisional assistance-gap index. Five testable hypotheses are formulated, and a three-arm randomised study with a preceding pilot and multi-context replication is proposed as future work. The framework has not been empirically validated, and no data were collected for this article.

items.title: Learning to Defer under Expert Drift
items.abstract: The learning to defer (L2D) framework enables safety in machine learning and AI systems by allocating difficult or critical decisions to a human expert. However, most prior work on L2D assumes fixed expert reliability, overlooking temporal fluctuations in human performance due to factors such as fatigue and cognitive biases. Humans commonly exhibit such substantial, systematic performance shifts across a wide range of domains, from high-stakes settings such as radiology, aviation, and judicial decision-making, to everyday tasks such as crowdsourced image annotation. We propose Expert-Drift-Adapted Learning-to-Defer (EDA-L2D), a novel expert-aware L2D framework that explicitly models these temporal shifts by conditioning the deferral head on recent histories of expert outcomes via a sequence model. This history-aware approach enables adaptive deferral policies that anticipate reliability fluctuations and better allocate decisions between human and machine over time. We provide comprehensive experiments across three diverse tasks -- image classification, medical diagnosis, and hate speech detection -- including generalization analyses under realistic deferral conditions and irregular shifts in expert reliability. Our results show that EDA-L2D adapts more effectively than prior L2D methods to diverse temporal patterns of expert reliability, resulting in improved system performance and more effective deferral decisions. Code is available at https://github.com/ZiyaoMou/L2D-Expert-Drift.

items.title: mPACT-MIS-v1.0: A Clinician–Informed Framework for Evaluating Epistemic Drift in Large Language Models
items.abstract: Introduction: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly shape how users evaluate information, form beliefs, and make decisions. Epistemic quality refers to the extent to which responses support accurate understanding, calibrated confidence, evidence-grounded beliefs, and independent reasoning. Risks extend beyond misinformation to reinforcing unsupported beliefs, expressing unwarranted certainty, and failing to challenge misleading assumptions. We developed mPACT-MIS-v1.0 to evaluate model behaviors that may support or undermine epistemic quality.Methods: We evaluated 60 expert-authored, multi-turn conversations (642 model turns; mean 10.70 [SD 2.70], range 5–17) across ten personas and six LLMs: Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini (2.5 Flash/3 Flash Preview), GPT-5.2, Grok 4.1, LLaMA 3.3 70B, and Mistral Medium 3. Trained annotators coded model turns using four helpful and four harmful behavioral labels informed by Self-Determination Theory and user turns for risky belief or behavior expressions. Model responses were classified as helpful-only, harmful-only, mixed, or uncoded. Conversation-averaged scores (0–10; higher is better) were calculated with 95% confidence intervals from conversation-clustered bootstrapping. Additional analyses examined responses to risk, transitions, correction latency, and persona variation.Results: Of 642 model turns, 261 (40.7%) were harmful-only, 78 (12.1%) mixed, 139 (21.7%) helpful-only, and 164 (25.5%) uncoded; 52.8% contained harmful behavior. Promoting risky beliefs or behaviors was the most frequent harmful label, while assessing risk was the least frequent helpful label (2.0%). Scores ranged from 2.60/10 (95% CI 1.68–4.04) for Mistral Medium 3 to 6.98/10 (95% CI 5.80–8.04) for Claude Sonnet 4.5, the only model with more helpful-only than harmful-only turns. Harmful behavior followed 74% of risky belief expressions and 73% of risky behavior expressions, versus 28% of turns without preceding risk expressions. Harmful responses often persisted: Claude recovered to helpful-only on 35% of transitions, versus 0–6% for four other models. Of 78 mixed responses, 77 combined a challenge to user beliefs or behaviors with harmful behavior. Performance varied substantially across personas.Discussion: Harmful responses frequently reinforced risky beliefs or behaviors, while support for independent reasoning was less common. Persistent harmful behavior, variable recovery, and mixed responses demonstrate why epistemic safety requires evaluation beyond factual accuracy or isolated outputs. Misinformation-related risks may arise through how models engage with users' beliefs over time. mPACT-MIS-v1.0 offers a behavioral framework for identifying potential reinforcement or correction, although it does not directly measure changes in users' beliefs or decisions.

items.title: Navigating the Ethical Landscape of AI in HRM: An Umbrella Review and Integrated Framework of Trust, Fairness, and Employee Well-being
items.abstract: Literature reviews on the ethics of artificial intelligence (AI) in human resource management (HRM) have multiplied quickly, and the result is an evidence base that is abundant but scattered. Practitioners seeking guidance grounded in evidence have nowhere consolidated to turn. This study addresses that problem through an umbrella review, conducted under Joanna Briggs Institute guidance and reported according to the PRISMA 2020 statement. A structured Scopus search produced a final corpus of thirteen peer-reviewed systematic and scoping reviews, published between 2020 and 2026. We analysed the corpus in two stages: a quantitative, descriptive mapping, then a six-phase qualitative thematic analysis. The mapping shows a field that consolidated only very recently; ten of the thirteen reviews appeared in 2025, and recruitment and selection dominate the contexts studied. Fairness is the concern the reviews examine most fully. Well-being is the one they examine least. The thematic analysis organised the evidence into three macro-themes, trust dynamics in AI-enabled HRM, algorithmic fairness and bias mitigation, and employee well-being and vulnerability, and showed that the literature has treated these as isolated questions. Our main contribution is the Integrated Ethical AI-HRM Framework, which orders the three pillars into a single structure: fairness and transparency condition employee trust, trust in turn shapes well-being, and the long-term durability of workplace AI depends on mitigating algorithmic bias and keeping algorithmic reasoning explainable.

This paper presents a decision-making method, leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs), to streamline the quantification of process quality metrics. By processing scenario descriptions, the LLM autonomously assigns metric values, enabling efficient, data-driven assessment of workstation configurations. The deployed system’s architecture, data pipeline, and prompt engineering strategy are also detailed. A case study from the household appliance sector is used to validate the approach leading to enhanced robustness, adaptability, and efficiency while also reducing manual engineering effort while supporting optimal workstation design.

items.title: Pandora's Toolbox Or Why Agent Safety Cannot Be Verified
items.abstract: Present artificial intelligence agents are constructed by means of a coupling between a fixed language model with a general computing device. We show that this coupling makes safety undecidable. In particular, we show that given some dangerous program, no algorithm can predict whether an agent will run such a program that is semantically equivalent. In general, guardrails, blacklists, whitelists and certifications can only lead to imperfect safety solutions. Under finite constraints (bounded context, values and running time) safety is decidable but still intractable. Specifically, the problem is $\mathsf{PSPACE}$-complete even when the description of the agent is known. Finally, safety is not a compositional property, i.e., agents that can be proven safe on their own can still produce unsafe behavior when grouped together. We also discuss relaxed notions of safety that could be used in practice.

items.title: Physician AI disclosure, condition severity, and public trust in digital medicine
items.abstract: Public trust is central to the implementation of artificial intelligence (AI) in digital medicine, yet little is known about how patients respond to different forms of physician AI disclosure across clinical risk contexts. In a 5 × 2 factorial experiment in mainland China, 1574 adults were randomly assigned to physician profiles varying by AI use type and condition severity. Administrative AI was rated more favorably than diagnostic and therapeutic AI across physician perception and care-seeking intention outcomes. High-severity conditions amplified negative responses to therapeutic AI, whereas explicit non-AI disclosure was associated with greater appointment willingness under high severity. Exploratory mediation analyses suggested that competence, trust, and empathy accounted for different disclosure-related response patterns. Main effects were directionally consistent in a supplementary offline community sample from Macao ( n = 128). These findings suggest that AI disclosure in digital medicine should distinguish administrative from clinical uses and be calibrated to clinical severity, while highlighting the need for preregistered replication using behavioral outcomes.

items.title: PlanWise: An AI-Powered Personal and Collaborative Task Management System
items.abstract: Effective task and project management needs efficient task prioritization, scheduling, progress monitoring, and coordination among people, all things considered. Conventional task management systems mostly rest on manual planning and tracking, which can make it difficult for users to manage competing priorities and changing workloads. This paper introduces PlanWise, an AI-powered personal and collaborative task management system designed to support task organization, project coordination, and intelligent productivity assistance, at least in principle. A web-based interface with backend services and database management is being blended by this setup to support personal tasks and collaborative project workflows, and includes large language model-based AI assistance for daily planning, task guidance, and project intelligence, combining task-related information and deterministic processing with AI-generated explanations and recommendations. It also is stressing user control by requiring approval for AI-suggested changes before they're employed. PlanWise is built using React and Vite for the frontend and Supabase for authentication, database operations, and backend functionality, with Google Gemini API integration for AI-assisted attributes. This paper is outlining the system architecture, design methodology, implementation approach, and evaluation framework. In fact, the current implementation founds for integrating AI assistance into the personal and collaborative task management. Further testing is required for the assessment of the reliability, potency and concrete benefits of its AI-driven capabilities. Keywords—Artificial Intelligence, Task Management, Project Management, Large Language Models, Intelligent Planning, Human-AI Interaction

items.title: Platform Versus Creator Provision of Generative AI on Creator Platforms
items.abstract: Generative AI is changing not only how content is created on digital content platforms but also who provides the AI used to create it. Platforms may offer generative AI using data pooled across creators, whereas creators may provide AI services based on their own content. Understanding how these provision regimes affect creators’ investment incentives and the value generated by AI is therefore important. We develop a game-theoretic model in which human-generated content competes with AI-generated content while contributing to AI learning. The results show that platform provision can induce higher human-generated content quality than creator provision when AI learning effectiveness lies within a certain range and the platform’s pooled-data advantage is limited. A stronger pooled-data advantage can make creator provision more favorable for sustaining human-generated content quality. Platform provision can nevertheless generate higher AI-generated content quality even when creator provision induces higher human-generated content quality, provided that the pooled-data advantage is sufficiently strong. We further find that AI value sharing can encourage or discourage quality investment under platform provision, while its effects on regime preferences and preference alignment depend on market conditions. Thus, the provision regime preferred by the creator need not be the one that sustains higher human-generated content quality.

items.title: PlayCraft: Designing Engaging Games from Agent Play Experience
items.abstract: Recent AI agents can generate playable games, but these games are not necessarily engaging. Mastery is a key source of engagement, yet designing for it requires extensive human play and tuning. We propose PlayCraft, an automated framework that uses a vision-based agent to play games and draws on its detailed play experience to revise them for mastery. Starting from an initial game, PlayCraft alternates between playing and crafting. In the playing stage, a player agent watches the game screen, uses the controls, and pursues the game objective over repeated episodes while retaining memory. After each episode, it reports its progress, outcomes, decisions, and reflections. In the crafting stage, a crafter agent uses these reports to revise the game. It estimates player abilities, predicts performance at different proficiency levels, and compares those predictions with a target learning progression. It diagnoses the game and addresses the gaps by giving players meaningful opportunities to improve through better decisions and execution. We evaluate games in fresh runs with player agents across three intelligence settings, measuring learning gain and learning slope. Compared with the initial games, PlayCraft yields larger learning gains and steeper learning slopes in most games. It also outperforms the baselines on the macro-average of each metric at every intelligence setting.

items.title: Pro$^2$ Agent: Scientific Problem Probing for Autonomous AI R&D
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can now autonomously conduct AI research by writing code and running experiments. They typically do so by iteratively optimizing a codebase, while ignoring the problem structure behind the task. This formulation is effective on simpler tasks, but on difficult problems it often gets stuck in the wrong solution region because the agent never explicitly represents its understanding of the problem. We introduce Pro$^2$ Agent, which shifts the primary state of autonomous AI research from a codebase state to a Problem State: an explicit structure of what problems prevent success and which solutions are likely to address them. Pro$^2$ Agent initializes the Problem State through comprehensive analysis of available resources and constraints. It then performs targeted research to relate the identified problems to candidate solutions. Through controlled hypothesis testing, the agent updates the importance of a suspected problem or the benefit brought by a candidate solution. On the complete MLE-Bench, Pro$^2$ Agent matches the best reported medal rate (70.7%) under the standard 24-hour budget and reaches 76.0% with a 48-hour budget, the highest medal rate reported on the complete benchmark. It also achieves competitive performance on PostTrainBench. In addition, it produces research notes for each task that make the research process transparent and reusable by human researchers.

items.abstract: This study aimed to determine the psychometric properties of the School Task Engagement Scale (ECTE) among primary school students from UGEL Santa, 2026. A basic, quantitative, non-experimental, cross-sectional study with a descriptive-instrumental scope was conducted. The sample consisted of 300 fourth-, fifth-, and sixth-grade students selected through proportional stratified probability sampling. Data were collected through a survey using the 18-item ECTE, which measures affective, behavioral, and cognitive engagement. Content validity was assessed by five experts, yielding an overall Aiken’s V of 1.00 for clarity, relevance, and coherence. The three-factor model showed acceptable fit indices (χ²/df = 2.18; RMSEA = 0.063; SRMR = 0.044; CFI = 0.921; TLI = 0.909), and factor loadings were above 0.50. Cronbach’s alpha values for the dimensions ranged from 0.765 to 0.787, while McDonald’s omega ranged from 0.766 to 0.792. The overall scale yielded α = 0.914 and ω = 0.916. The findings provide favorable evidence of validity and reliability in the studied sample, although generalization to other populations requires further research.

items.title: Psychological reward and physiological demand in virtual cycling: an exploratory within-subject study
items.abstract: Virtual environments are often added to exercise equipment to make exercise more engaging, although previous work has often emphasised enjoyment. This exploratory within-subject study compared stationary cycling with screen-based virtual cycling in 15 adults (6 women, 9 men; aged 20–59 years). Each participant completed one 10-min, self-paced session in each condition, in counterbalanced order, on the same recumbent bicycle with fixed resistance. After each session, participants completed the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory and rated their perceived exertion (Borg 6–20); heart rate and cadence were recorded every minute. Enjoyment was higher after virtual cycling (mean difference 2.31 points on a 1–7 scale, 95% CI [1.61, 3.00]), as was value/usefulness (1.38 [0.56, 2.20]); 14 and 12 participants, respectively, reported higher scores. Both paired t-test differences remained after Holm correction. Differences in perceived competence, effort/importance, and pressure/tension were smaller, with confidence intervals including zero. Heart rate (4.9 bpm, 95% CI [-0.04, 9.8]) and cadence (2.8 rpm [-2.4, 7.9]) showed no clear difference between conditions. Perceived exertion was slightly higher during virtual cycling (0.8 points [0.01, 1.59]), but this difference did not remain after correction. Power output was not measured, so workload could not be compared directly. Enjoyment was strongly correlated with value/usefulness during virtual cycling (r = 0.87, 95% CI [0.64, 0.95]); individual responses also varied, particularly in perceived competence. Given the small sample and single 10-min session per condition, larger studies should measure workload directly and examine responses across repeated sessions.
